newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Nobel Peace winners react differently to award.
newsitem.headline: Nobel Peace winners react differently to award.

text.p: The two East Timorese men who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday had differing reactions to the award, one hoping for reconciliation in the troubled territory, the other seeing it as a boost for independence from Indonesia.

East Timor Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo said he hoped the award would bolster efforts to bring peace to the former Portuguese colony but Jose Ramos-Horta, the Australia-based Timorese resistance leader, said it should be a signal to Indonesia to quit.
"We have to work hard for peace," Belo, 51, told Reuters by telephone from the territory's capital Dili, some 2,000 km (1,250 miles) east of Jakarta.
"I see it (the award) as a victory for East Timorese...and all Indonesians," he said.
"Sometimes they (the government) understand and accept there is a need for love and dialogue. (I am) sometimes happy with the process...sometimes not, but it (the process) needs time," he said.

Ramos-Horta said he hoped the Peace Prize would send a message to Indonesia "that the people of East Timor have suffered long enough and that there must be serious dialogue under United Nations auspices to resolve the problem".
"I am prepared, as I have said again and again, to fly to Indonesia for informal discussions," he added.
Norwegian Nobel Committee Chairman Francis Sejersted said Belo and Ramos-Horta shared the prize "for their work towards a just and peaceful solution to the conflict in East Timor".

"Belo...has been the foremost representative of the people of East Timor. At the risk of his own life, he has tried to protect his people from infringements by those in power," the committee said in a statement.
The committe said Ramos-Horta "has been the leading international spokesman for East Timor's cause since 1975 when Indonesia took control of East Timor".
Speaking to Reuters from his mother's home in Sydney, Ramos-Horta, 46, also said that the prize should not have gone to him, but to jailed East Timor resistance leader Xanana Gusmao.
"I would feel much happier if instead of my name, his was selected," he said.
Gusmao, who was leading military resistance to Jakarta's rule in East Timor, was captured in 1992 and is serving a 20-year jail sentence in Indonesia.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975, just after Portugal pulled out, and annexed the territory a year later. The annexation has never been recognised by the United Nations.
Ramos-Horta, who was secretary for foreign affairs and information in the Fretilin movement, fled the territory three days before Indonesia's invasion.

Belo, who once accused Moslem-majority Indonesia of turning East Timor into hell through constant arrests and intimidation and by spreading Islam among the territory's mainly-Catholic residents, said the award made his responsibilities heavier.
"...Because there will be many questions, criticism and suspicion," he said without elaborating. "It is better that I had not won. It makes my responsibilities heavier."
Belo also said that Indonesia's iron grip on East Timor needed to be relaxed.
"(Indonesia) has to listen to the aspirations of East Timorese. Their (Timorese) dignity should be given priority."
He said that if possible East Timor should be given autonomy, adding that there should be continued dialogue between East Timorese and the Indonesian government.

"I am prepared to continue holding dialogues as long as they (government) are prepared to listen," he said. "There is some openness but it is very little. Hopefully, with the passage of time, there will be more."

Asked whether he planned to meet President Suharto when he visits East Timor next Tuesday to inaugurate several public projects, including a bronze statue of Jesus Christ said to be the second largest in the world, Belo said: "If I am invited (to meet him), I will."
